lessons.title: Herr Ali lebte in Zürich: life events and the regular Präteritum
lessons.goal: Name life events and read and write a short life story with regular verbs in the Präteritum, including -ete, separable and reflexive verbs.

grammar.point: Regular verbs build the Präteritum with stem + -te + person ending: ich lebte, du lebtest, er lebte, wir lebten, ihr lebtet, sie lebten. Stems ending in -t, -d, -chn or -ffn insert an e: arbeitete, gründete, eröffnete. Separable verbs split (er wanderte aus) and sich stays next to the verb.
grammar.oneLine: Herr Ali lebte in Zürich und arbeitete in einem Hotel.

mistake.why: After a stem that ends in -t (or -d, -chn, -ffn) the -te is hard to say, so German inserts an e: arbeit-e-te.

terms.meaning: the one-word past of writing and stories: lebte, arbeitete, kam
the verb without -en: leb-, arbeit-, wohn-
turning point: a moment that changes a life

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich war in Wien' to 'Ich lebte in Wien'
cards.body: This chapter is called Veränderungen (changes). Mira and Leon plan a radio programme called „Wendepunkte“ (turning points), and Herr Ali will be a guest. His life story uses the Präteritum, the one-word past of stories. You already know it for sein, haben and the modals.
steps: You already know: Herr Ali war jung. Er hatte wenig Geld. One word each: war, hatte.
New today: Herr Ali lebte in Zürich. Er arbeitete in einem Hotel. The same one-word past, now for normal verbs: stem + -te.
By the end you can: name life events and tell a short life story with regular verbs, also with -ete, separable and reflexive verbs.

examples.de: Herr Ali war jung.
examples.en: Herr Ali was young.
examples.why: You know this: war is the one-word past of sein.

examples.de: Er hatte wenig Geld.
examples.en: He had little money.
examples.why: You know this too: hatte is the one-word past of haben.

examples.de: Herr Ali lebte in Zürich.
examples.en: Herr Ali lived in Zürich.
examples.why: New today: the same idea for a normal verb. leben becomes lebte.

cards.more: Imagine two kinds of past in your head. The first one is the Perfekt, which you use when you chat: hat gelebt, hat gearbeitet. The second one is a shorter, calmer past that you find in books, newspapers and biographies. You already met three tiny pieces of it: war, hatte and the modals. Today we make the same short past for ordinary verbs. The recipe is friendly: the verb stem plus -te. One word, no helper verb, and it sounds like a story.

cards.title: Life events: from Geburt to Rente
cards.body: Every life has signposts: birth, youth, training, love, separation, a move to another country, retirement. The Lebensphasen follow each other: Kindheit, Jugend, erwachsen sein, Rente. A moment that changes everything is a Wendepunkt. Learn each event as a noun and as a verb phrase.
cards.lead: Before any grammar we need the vocabulary of a life story. This card gives you the big events as nouns and as verb phrases, so you can name what happens in a life.

examples.de: Mit 18 ist man erwachsen.
examples.en: At 18 you are an adult.

examples.de: Nach der Schule machen viele eine Lehre.
examples.en: After school many people do an apprenticeship.

examples.de: Mit 67 geht man in Rente.
examples.en: At 67 you retire.

deeper.text: To say where and when you were born, German uses geboren with werden: Ich wurde in Wien geboren. Wurde is the Präteritum of werden, which you already know. In speech you also hear Ich bin in Wien geboren with sein. Both are correct. The questions are Wo wurdest du geboren? and Wo bist du geboren?

example.de: Mira wurde in Wien geboren.
example.en: Mira was born in Vienna.

cards.more: Picture a train line with stations. Station one is die Geburt, then die Jugend, then a job, maybe a partner, maybe a move to another country, at the end die Rente. The nouns are the names on the station signs. The verbs tell you what a person does there: heiraten, sich trennen, in Rente gehen. When you tell a life story, you ride the line from left to right. Learn the nouns and the verbs in pairs, then you can name the signpost and say what happens at it.

cards.title: The -te signal: leben becomes lebte
cards.body: The regular Präteritum is a short recipe: take the infinitive, cut -en, add -te, then add the person ending. Leben becomes leb- and then lebte. Ich and er/sie/es have the same form, like war and konnte. All other persons add the ending you expect.
cards.lead: You have met war, hatte and konnte. Here is the recipe that makes the same kind of one-word past for normal verbs, step by step and for every person.
steps: 1. Start with the infinitive: leben
2. Cut off -en: leb-
3. Add the signal -te: lebte
4. Add the person ending: du lebtest, wir lebten, ihr lebtet

examples.de: Herr Ali lebte in Zürich.
examples.en: Herr Ali lived in Zürich.

examples.de: Wir wohnten in einer kleinen Stadt.
examples.en: We lived in a small town.

examples.de: Mira wohnte früher in Wien.
examples.en: Mira used to live in Vienna.

deeper.text: Wir lebten and sie lebten look identical, and so does the polite Sie lebten. The sentence around the verb tells you who is meant. In the present the -t of er lebt shows the person, but in the Präteritum the -te belongs to every person and only the ending after it changes. So the -te is the signal for past, and the ending still tells you who.

example.de: Wo lebten Sie als Kind, Herr Ali?
example.en: Where did you live as a child, Herr Ali?

cards.more: Think of -te as a little flag that waves: this happened earlier. The verb stem is the body, the flag is -te, and the last bit is a name tag for the person. In the present you say lebe, lebst, lebt. In the past the flag is added to everyone: leb + te + st gives lebtest. Ich and er/sie/es wear no name tag, so they look identical. English does something similar with -ed: I lived, she lived. German just keeps the name tag for du, wir, ihr and sie.

cards.title: Hard to say? Insert an e: arbeitete
cards.body: Some stems end in t, d, chn or ffn. Then the plain -te is hard to say: arbeitte sounds wrong. German inserts an e: arbeit-e-te. The same e appears before the person endings: du arbeitetest, wir arbeiteten. If lebte flows and arbeitte stumbles, add the e.
cards.lead: So far -te was easy. Some verbs need a helper vowel before it. This card shows which stems need it and why, so you can build the right form every time.

examples.de: Herr Ali arbeitete in einem Hotel.
examples.en: Herr Ali worked in a hotel.

examples.de: Er eröffnete ein Restaurant.
examples.en: He opened a restaurant.

examples.de: Sie heirateten im Sommer.
examples.en: They got married in the summer.

deeper.text: The e only protects stems that are hard to pronounce: -t, -d, and a consonant plus n such as -chn, -ffn or -gn (regnen becomes regnete). Stems ending in l, r or n after a vowel need no help: lernen becomes lernte, wohnen becomes wohnte, wandern becomes wanderte. Ask yourself if the -te can be said easily, and trust your mouth.

example.de: Es regnete den ganzen Tag.
example.en: It rained all day.

cards.more: Say it aloud. Lebte is one beat plus te, easy. Now try arbeitte: your tongue trips over the double t. Say arbeitete instead: ar-bei-te-te, four smooth beats. German adds an e exactly where two sounds would crash into each other. English has the same trick: you say want-ed, not wantd. So the extra e is not a strange exception, it is a helper for your mouth. Rule of thumb: if you cannot say the form, put an e in the middle.

cards.title: Separable and reflexive verbs: the pieces split
cards.body: Separable verbs split in the Präteritum like in the present. The changed verb stays in position 2, the prefix goes to the very end. The -te sits on the main verb only. Reflexive verbs keep sich close to the verb: Er verliebte sich. Sie trennten sich.
cards.lead: You know split verbs and sich from the present. This card shows that the Präteritum uses the same frame, so you only add -te and keep the order you already know.

rows: Sie hörte um fünf Uhr auf.

examples.de: Herr Ali wanderte nach Berlin aus.
examples.en: Herr Ali emigrated to Berlin.

examples.de: Wir kauften im Supermarkt ein.
examples.en: We did the shopping at the supermarket.

examples.de: Die beiden trennten sich.
examples.en: The two of them split up.

deeper.text: In a weil-clause the two pieces of a separable verb join again and the whole verb goes to the end, now with -te: weil er auswanderte. This is the same rule as in the present (weil er auswandert). The Präteritum only changes the verb ending. The word order in main and side clauses stays exactly the same.

example.de: Er war traurig, weil er aus der Schweiz auswanderte.
example.en: He was sad because he emigrated from Switzerland.

cards.more: Think of a zipper. In a main clause the zipper is open: wanderte … aus. The two halves are far apart, one in position 2, one at the end. Never zip them together in a main clause: Er auswanderte nach Berlin is wrong. The little word sich is like a shadow. It stays right behind the verb or the subject: Er verliebte sich, sie trennten sich. Say the pairs aloud: wanderte-aus, kauften-ein, hörte-auf. The first half carries the -te, the last half stays plain.

cards.title: Herr Ali's Lebenslauf: a life in six sentences
cards.body: Here is the model story of this chapter: Herr Ali, from Zürich to Berlin. Read the timeline first, then the six sentences. Notice that every verb is regular and ends in -te. The years stay vague, in the way people tell it: mit 16, vor über 20 Jahren.
cards.lead: Now everything works together. You read a mini biography with regular -te verbs, one separable verb, and a time word at the start of most sentences.
steps: Kindheit: Zürich
Mit 16: Lehre als Koch
Dann: Hotel in Basel
Mit 25: auswandern nach Berlin
2010: das Restaurant „Zum Löwen“

examples.de: Herr Ali lebte als Kind in Zürich.
examples.en: Herr Ali lived in Zürich as a child.

examples.de: Mit 16 machte er eine Lehre als Koch.
examples.en: At 16 he did an apprenticeship as a cook.

examples.de: Dann arbeitete er in einem Hotel in Basel.
examples.en: Then he worked in a hotel in Basel.

examples.de: Mit 25 wanderte er nach Berlin aus.
examples.en: At 25 he emigrated to Berlin.

examples.de: Das war ein Wendepunkt in seinem Leben.
examples.en: That was a turning point in his life.

examples.de: 2010 eröffnete er das Restaurant „Zum Löwen“.
examples.en: In 2010 he opened the restaurant „Zum Löwen“.

deeper.text: A time word in first position pushes the subject behind the verb: Mit 16 machte er eine Lehre, never Mit 16 er machte. The verb stays in position 2. You know this from the present. A life story uses it all the time, because almost every sentence starts with when: dann, mit 25, nach der Lehre. It makes the story flow like a timeline.

example.de: Nach der Lehre arbeitete er zwei Jahre in einem Hotel.
example.en: After the apprenticeship he worked in a hotel for two years.

cards.more: Read the text like a film in six frames. Frame one: a child in Zürich. Frame two: a teenager in a hot kitchen. Frame three: a young cook in a hotel. Frame four: a train to Berlin, and the feeling that now everything changes. Frame five: the sign „Zum Löwen“ above a door. Every frame is one sentence with one -te verb, and a time word shows when. Now try to retell the film with five verbs only: lebte, machte, arbeitete, wanderte … aus, eröffnete.

cards.title: Where you read the Präteritum
cards.body: The Präteritum is the language of writing: biographies, newspaper reports, Wikipedia pages, a written Lebenslauf and stories. When people talk, they usually choose the Perfekt. You do not have to decide yet: today you learn to recognise and to write the Präteritum. The choice between the two comes in a later lesson.
cards.lead: Why learn a past that people rarely speak? Because you meet it every time you read. This card shows where it lives, so you know what to look for in a text.

rows: Die Stadt eröffnete ein neues Schwimmbad.
Die Malerin wohnte lange in Wien und malte dort viele Bilder.
Er machte eine Lehre und arbeitete in einem Hotel.

examples.de: Der Verein feierte ein Fest.
examples.en: The club held a party.

examples.de: Die Familie wohnte zehn Jahre in Basel.
examples.en: The family lived in Basel for ten years.

deeper.text: English gives you a good map: play – played, live – lived, work – worked. German -te corresponds to English -ed. One difference: English uses played for every person, but German keeps a person ending after -te: ich spielte, du spieltest, wir spielten. So whenever you see -te followed by an ending, think past tense plus person.

example.de: Wir spielten früher oft Karten.
example.en: We often used to play cards.

cards.more: Look at English first. Play, played. Live, lived. Work, worked. One ending, -ed, for every person. German has the same idea: -te is the German -ed. The only extra is the name tag: ich spielte, du spieltest, wir spielten. You will spot these forms quickly in a text, because they are the verbs that carry the story. Here is a small experiment: take any newspaper article and underline every -te verb. In a minute you can follow the plot without reading the rest.

lessons.title: Er kam nach Berlin: irregular verbs in the Präteritum
lessons.goal: Tell a life story with the most common irregular verbs: new stem, no -te, and the right endings, also for separable verbs and es gab.

grammar.point: Irregular verbs change their stem and take no -te: kommen becomes kam. Ich and er/sie/es have no ending (ich kam, er kam), du adds -st (kamst), wir and sie add -en (kamen), ihr adds -t (kamt). Separable verbs split (er kam an), and es gab is the Präteritum of es gibt.
grammar.oneLine: Mit 25 verließ er die Schweiz und fuhr nach Berlin.

mistake.why: Irregular verbs have a new stem and no -te. Ich and er/sie/es take no ending at all: ich kam, er kam.

terms.meaning: a verb with a new stem in the Präteritum and no -te: kommen, kam
the principal parts of a verb: infinitive, Präteritum, Perfekt (gehen, ging, ist gegangen)
there was, there were: the Präteritum of es gibt

cards.title: Before we start: from 'ist gekommen' to 'kam'
cards.body: Last time Herr Ali lived in Zürich and worked in Basel, all with regular -te verbs. Today he leaves and arrives in Berlin. Many of the most common verbs, such as kommen, gehen and finden, do not take -te. They change the stem. The Perfekt participle you already know is a good hint.
steps: You already know: Er ist nach Berlin gekommen. And: Er lebte in Zürich. The participle gekommen shows the vowel o.
New today: Er kam nach Berlin. A new stem, one word, no -te.
By the end you can: use the most common irregular verbs in the Präteritum, with all endings, with separable verbs and with es gab.

examples.de: Herr Ali ist nach Berlin gekommen.
examples.en: Herr Ali has come to Berlin.
examples.why: You know this: the Perfekt with sein and the participle at the end.

examples.de: Herr Ali lebte in Zürich.
examples.en: Herr Ali lived in Zürich.
examples.why: You know this too: a regular verb with -te.

examples.de: Herr Ali kam nach Berlin.
examples.en: Herr Ali came to Berlin.
examples.why: New today: kommen changes its stem to kam. No -te.

cards.more: Think of two groups of verbs. The first group is easy and polite: they only add -te, like leben, lebte. The second group is more independent: they change their vowel and add nothing. Kommen, kam. Fahren, fuhr. Finden, fand. These verbs are very common, so you will meet them in every story. Good news: you already know part of the secret. The vowel in the Perfekt participle often hints at the vowel in the Präteritum, for example gefahren, fuhr.

cards.title: Irregular verbs have a new stem
cards.body: Irregular verbs change their stem in the Präteritum, and no -te is added. You have to learn the new stem, ideally together with the Perfekt, because a verb has three forms: infinitive, Präteritum, Perfekt. The table shows nine very common verbs. Notice which ones take sein in the Perfekt.
cards.lead: Regular verbs followed a recipe. These verbs follow a list. This card gives you nine of the most common ones with all three forms, so you can learn them as one block.

examples.de: Er ging oft in die Küche.
examples.en: He often went into the kitchen.

examples.de: Er fuhr mit dem Zug.
examples.en: He travelled by train.

examples.de: Sie schrieb eine lange E-Mail.
examples.en: She wrote a long email.

deeper.text: German teachers call the three forms the Stammformen: infinitive, Präteritum, Partizip II. Learn them as one set on one flash card: gehen – ging – ist gegangen. Always add the helper verb, because it belongs to the set: ist gegangen, but hat gesehen. If you know the three forms, you can build the Perfekt and the Präteritum without hesitation.

example.de: Sie sah den Zug nicht.
example.en: She did not see the train.

cards.more: Imagine each verb as a small family photo with three faces: the infinitive, the Präteritum and the Perfekt. Gehen, ging, gegangen. If you look only at one face, you might forget the others. If you look at the whole photo, the three faces help each other, because the vowels often match. Make ten flash cards, one family photo per card. Say the three forms aloud and add ist or hat. After a week, the nine verbs in this table will feel like old friends.

cards.title: The endings: ich kam, du kamst, wir kamen
cards.body: Irregular verbs have no -te, so the endings sit directly on the new stem. Ich and er/sie/es have no ending, which means they look like the bare stem: ich kam, er kam. Du adds -st, wir and sie add -en, ihr adds -t. Never add an e to ich: kame is wrong.
cards.lead: You know the new stems. Now you attach the person endings. This card compares two verbs, so you can see that the endings are the same for every irregular verb.

examples.de: Ich kam um acht Uhr.
examples.en: I came at eight o'clock.

examples.de: Du kamst zu spät.
examples.en: You came too late.

examples.de: Wir fuhren nach Basel.
examples.en: We drove to Basel.

deeper.text: Stems ending in -d or -t add an e before -st and -t, exactly like in the last lesson. So finden becomes du fandest and ihr fandet, and stehen becomes du standest. The forms ich fand, er fand and wir fanden need no extra e. The e only appears where two consonants would clash, so the rule you know from arbeitete works here too.

example.de: Du fandest ein kleines Zimmer.
example.en: You found a small room.

cards.more: Regular verbs wore a flag, the -te. Irregular verbs wear no flag at all. The only signal that says this is the past is the new vowel: ich kam, not ich komme. After that, the endings are almost the same as in the present. Du has -st, wir has -en, ihr has -t. Ich and er/sie/es have nothing. Read it aloud: ich kam, er kam, sie kam. The same three words, and that makes it easier than the present, where you need lebe, lebt, lebt.

cards.title: Vowel families: a memory help
cards.body: You do not have to learn 25 single verbs. Many of them fall into vowel families, with the same change inside a group. Learn one family at a time and say the verbs in a row. The table groups the verbs of this chapter. A few verbs are loners, and you simply learn them by heart.
cards.lead: Twenty-five new stems sound like a lot. This card sorts them into small families by their vowel, so you learn patterns first and single verbs second.

rows: finden – fand, trinken – trank, beginnen – begann
sprechen – sprach, treffen – traf, nehmen – nahm, sehen – sah, lesen – las, essen – aß, geben – gab
laufen – lief, verlassen – verließ, anfangen – fing an
gehen – ging, stehen – stand, sitzen – saß, ziehen – zog, kommen – kam, verstehen – verstand

examples.de: Er blieb in Berlin.
examples.en: He stayed in Berlin.

examples.de: Sie sprach mit dem Chef.
examples.en: She spoke with the boss.

examples.de: Wir tranken Tee.
examples.en: We drank tea.

deeper.text: Some families even show all three forms in one pattern. The ei family is ei – ie – ie: bleiben, blieb, geblieben and schreiben, schrieb, geschrieben. The i family is i – a – u: finden, fand, gefunden and trinken, trank, getrunken. So if you know one verb of the family, you can guess the Perfekt participle of a new verb of the same family.

example.de: Wir tranken Tee und blieben lange.
example.en: We drank tea and stayed a long time.

cards.more: Imagine a class photo where the verbs stand in groups. In the first row all the ei-verbs hold hands and jump to ie: bleiben, blieb. In the second row the i-verbs all become a: finden, fand, trinken, trank. The e-verbs in the third row also become a: sprechen, sprach. The ear loves rhymes, so say each row like a poem. Do not learn all of them today: pick one row, say it five times, then use it in a sentence about your own day.

cards.title: Separable irregular verbs: kam … an, fing … an
cards.body: Separable verbs split in the Präteritum exactly like in the present. The Präteritum stem stands in position 2, the prefix goes to the very end. Ankommen becomes Er kam an. The Perfekt has ge in the middle: angekommen. The Präteritum has no ge at all, which makes it shorter.
cards.lead: Many of Herr Ali's verbs are separable. You know the split from the present and from the regular verbs. Here it is with the new stems, so the frame stays the same.

examples.de: Er kam in Berlin an.
examples.en: He arrived in Berlin.

examples.de: Er wuchs in Zürich auf.
examples.en: He grew up in Zürich.

examples.de: Sie zogen nach Berlin um.
examples.en: They moved to Berlin.

deeper.text: Not every prefix splits. Verbs with be-, ver-, ent-, er- and ge- never split, because the prefix is not stressed: verlassen becomes Er verließ die Schweiz, and beginnen becomes Der Film begann um acht. Compare ankommen, which splits, and verlassen, which does not. If the first syllable is stressed (AN-kommen), the verb is separable.

example.de: Der Film begann um acht Uhr.
example.en: The film started at eight o'clock.

cards.more: Think of two Lego bricks. In the Perfekt they are glued together in the middle: an-ge-kommen. In the Präteritum you pull the bricks apart: kam on one end of the sentence, an on the other end. The mistake to avoid is to glue them again in a main clause: Er ankam in Berlin is wrong. The right sentence is Er kam in Berlin an. And the Präteritum has an advantage: there is no ge-, so you only need the stem. That is less to remember.

cards.title: Es gab: there was, there were
cards.body: Es gibt means there is or there are. In the past it becomes es gab: there was or there were. The form does not change for singular or plural, and the thing that exists is in the accusative: Es gab einen Bahnhof, es gab keine Schule. In a question, es follows the verb: Gab es …?
cards.lead: Stories do not only tell what people did, they also describe what existed. This card teaches the past of es gibt, one small form with many uses.

examples.de: Damals gab es in seiner Straße kein Schweizer Restaurant.
examples.en: At that time there was no Swiss restaurant on his street.

examples.de: Es gab viele alte Häuser und kleine Läden.
examples.en: There were many old houses and small shops.
parts: viele alte Häuser und kleine Läden.

examples.de: Gab es einen Bahnhof in der Nähe?
examples.en: Was there a station nearby?

deeper.text: Es gab is the normal form in everyday speech, not only in writing. People say Es gab ein Problem, and they say it in a chat. The word es is a placeholder subject, not a person, so you cannot replace it with another subject. In the sentence Damals gab es kein Internet the verb stays in position 2 and es moves behind it.

example.de: Gab es damals schon Handys?
example.en: Were there mobile phones at that time already?

cards.more: Imagine an old photo of Herr Ali's street. You point at it and say: there was a bakery, there was a small park, there was no Swiss restaurant. In German you only need two words: es gab. In English you must choose between there was and there were, but German always says es gab, singular or plural. Es is not a person. It is just a small helper that makes the sentence work. Compare es gibt for today, es gab for the photo.

cards.title: Herr Ali's story continues: arriving in Berlin
cards.body: Now Herr Ali leaves Switzerland. Read the six sentences with the timeline. Every verb is irregular, and one of them is separable. Notice that the sentences with a time word first put the verb in position 2, exactly as in lesson 1. The years stay vague.
cards.lead: This card puts the new verbs into a story. Look for the verb in every sentence and say its infinitive. That is the best way to check that you can go from kam back to kommen.
steps: Mit 25: die Schweiz verlassen
Mit dem Zug nach Berlin fahren
Im Winter ankommen
Ein kleines Zimmer finden
Den Dialekt kaum verstehen
In der Küche viele Leute treffen

examples.de: Mit 25 verließ er die Schweiz.
examples.en: At 25 he left Switzerland.

examples.de: Er fuhr mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
examples.en: He went to Berlin by train.

examples.de: Er kam im Winter an.
examples.en: He arrived in the winter.

examples.de: Er fand ein kleines Zimmer.
examples.en: He found a small room.

examples.de: Er verstand den Berliner Dialekt am Anfang kaum.
examples.en: At first he hardly understood the Berlin dialect.

examples.de: Er traf viele neue Leute in der Küche.
examples.en: He met many new people in the kitchen.

deeper.text: Berliner is not a noun here but an adjective made from a city name. Such adjectives end in -er and never change: der Berliner Dialekt, die Berliner Luft, Wiener Kaffeehäuser, Schweizer Käse. They are written with a capital letter. You can make them from almost every city, which is practical for describing where something comes from.

example.de: Er aß Schweizer Käse und trank Tee.
example.en: He ate Swiss cheese and drank tea.

cards.more: Read the six sentences like pictures in a photo album. First picture: a young cook with a suitcase at the border. Second picture: a train window, grey fields, snow. Third picture: the station in Berlin, cold hands. Fourth picture: a tiny room with one lamp. Fifth picture: a man who hardly understands a word of the local slang. Sixth picture: a busy kitchen and new faces. The Präteritum turns this album into one short story.

lessons.title: Damals dachte ich …: denken, wissen, bringen, nennen and a life story
lessons.goal: Use the five mixed verbs (dachte, wusste, brachte, nannte, kannte) and read and retell a whole life story in the Präteritum, with the Präsens for today.

grammar.topic: Mixed verbs in the Präteritum (dachte, wusste, brachte, nannte, kannte)
grammar.point: Mixed verbs change their vowel and add -te: denken – dachte, wissen – wusste, bringen – brachte, nennen – nannte, kennen – kannte. The endings are those of the regular verbs: ich dachte, du dachtest, wir dachten. The Perfekt participle has the same vowel: gedacht, gewusst, gebracht, genannt, gekannt.
grammar.oneLine: Damals dachte ich an Zürich, aber ich wusste, dass ich bleiben wollte.

mistake.right: Ich dachte, dass es schwer ist.
mistake.why: Denken is a mixed verb: it changes the vowel (denk- becomes dach-) and then adds -te. The form denkte does not exist.

terms.meaning: a verb with a new vowel and -te in the Präteritum: denken, dachte
nickname: a name friends or colleagues give someone
tense: Präsens, Perfekt, Präteritum

cards.title: Before we start: regular, irregular, and both at once
cards.body: So far Herr Ali lived, worked and came. Today we finish the picture of his story. Some verbs mix the two types: they change the vowel and add -te. These are only five verbs, but they are very common: denken, wissen, bringen, nennen and kennen. Then you read and retell a whole life story.
steps: You already know: Er lebte in Zürich (regular, -te). Er kam nach Berlin (irregular, new stem).
New today: Er dachte oft an Zürich. New vowel AND -te: dachte.
By the end you can: use the five mixed verbs and read and retell a life story with damals, zunächst, später, schließlich and heute.

examples.de: Er lebte in Zürich.
examples.en: He lived in Zürich.
examples.why: You know this: regular, stem + -te.

examples.de: Er kam nach Berlin.
examples.en: He came to Berlin.
examples.why: You know this too: irregular, a new stem and no -te.

examples.de: Er dachte oft an Zürich.
examples.en: He often thought of Zürich.
examples.why: New today: a new vowel and -te together.

cards.more: Imagine two kinds of runners. The weak runner keeps the same shoes and only puts on a number: lebte. The strong runner changes the shoes and puts on no number: kam. Five special runners do both. They change their shoes and wear a number: dachte, wusste, brachte, nannte, kannte. They are not many, so you can learn them all in one lesson. And since the number is the familiar -te, you only have to remember the new vowel.

cards.title: Mixed verbs: new vowel and -te
cards.body: Mixed verbs mix both types. They change the vowel like irregular verbs, and they take -te like regular verbs. A memory hook: the vowel changes like a strong verb, the ending -te comes from a weak verb. The Perfekt participle has the same vowel as the Präteritum: gedacht, gebracht, gekannt.
cards.lead: Regular verbs add -te, irregular verbs change the vowel. This card shows five verbs that do both and gives you a hook to remember them as one group.

examples.de: Er dachte oft an Zürich.
examples.en: He often thought of Zürich.

examples.de: Wir wussten das nicht.
examples.en: We did not know that.

examples.de: Sie brachte einen Kuchen.
examples.en: She brought a cake.

deeper.text: German has only about ten mixed verbs, so the group is small. Besides the five of this lesson there are, for example, brennen (brannte) and rennen (rannte). You do not need them now. The ending always follows the regular pattern: ich dachte, du dachtest, wir dachten, ihr dachtet. Only the stem is special. Learn the stem and you have the verb.

example.de: Wir brachten Blumen mit.
example.en: We brought flowers.

cards.more: Think of a cocktail. One half comes from the strong verbs, the other half from the weak verbs. From the strong verbs you take the new vowel: denken, dachte. From the weak verbs you take the -te. Five drinks only. Say them like a small poem: denken dachte, bringen brachte, kennen kannte, nennen nannte, wissen wusste. Then look at the Perfekt: gedacht, gebracht, gekannt, genannt, gewusst. The vowel is the same as in the Präteritum, so the participle helps you to remember.

cards.title: Wissen in the Präteritum
cards.body: Wissen is the most useful mixed verb. Present: ich weiß. Past: ich wusste. After wusste, a dass-clause or a question word often follows, and the verb goes to the end. The questions are Wusstest du, dass …? and Ich wusste nicht, wann …. The endings are the regular ones.
cards.lead: Of the five mixed verbs, wissen is the one you will use most. This card shows the whole conjugation next to the present, and how it connects with a side sentence.

examples.de: Ich wusste nicht, dass Herr Ali aus Zürich kam.
examples.en: I did not know that Herr Ali came from Zürich.

examples.de: Wusstest du, dass er Koch war?
examples.en: Did you know that he was a cook?

examples.de: Wir wussten nichts davon.
examples.en: We knew nothing about it.

deeper.text: In conversation people also say wusste, not hat gewusst: Das wusste ich nicht! is the natural answer. It is the same with war, hatte and the modals, which you already use in the Präteritum when you speak. Wissen belongs to this small group of verbs that stay in the short past even in a chat. A later lesson explains why.

example.de: Das wusste ich nicht!
example.en: I did not know that!

cards.more: Think of wissen as a pocket full of facts in your head. In the present the pocket says weiß, a strange form with ß. In the past the pocket says wusste, and the u is the new vowel. After wusste you usually say what you did or did not know, and that part is a side sentence: Ich wusste nicht, wann der Zug kam. The comma is automatic, and the verb jumps to the end. To say 'I did not know', answer Ich wusste nicht.

cards.title: Nennen, kennen, bringen: three small jobs
cards.body: Nennen means to call or to name: Sie nannten ihn Chef. The person is in the accusative, the name is a second accusative. Kennen means to know a person or a place. Bringen means to bring; with mit it splits: Er brachte ein Rezept mit. Each verb has its own small job.
cards.lead: The other three mixed verbs each do a different job. This card gives you one typical sentence for each, taken from Herr Ali's kitchen and his arrival in Berlin.

rows: In der Küche nannten ihn alle „Chef“.
Er brachte ein Rezept von seiner Großmutter mit.

examples.de: In der Küche nannten ihn alle „Chef“.
examples.en: In the kitchen everybody called him „Chef“.

examples.de: Wie nannte man dich als Kind?
examples.en: What did people call you as a child?

examples.de: Er kannte in Berlin niemanden.
examples.en: He did not know anybody in Berlin.

examples.de: Er brachte ein Rezept von seiner Großmutter mit.
examples.en: He brought a recipe from his grandmother.

deeper.text: Kennen and wissen both mean to know, but they do different jobs. Kennen goes with people, places and things you are familiar with: Ich kannte Zürich gut. Wissen goes with facts and usually with a dass-clause or a question word: Ich wusste, wo der Bahnhof war. English has only one verb, so this contrast needs practice.

example.de: Sie kannte die Stadt nicht, aber sie wusste, wo der Bahnhof war.
example.en: She did not know the city, but she knew where the station was.

cards.more: Picture the kitchen of „Zum Löwen“ twenty-five years ago. The new cook is quiet and works fast. The others do not use his name. They give him a nickname, and the verb for that is nennen: they called him Chef. Now picture the new cook at the station: he knew nobody in this city, kennen. He brought one thing from home, a recipe, and the verb is bringen, here with mit. Three little scenes, three little verbs, all with -te and a new vowel.

cards.title: Reading: „Vom Zürichsee an die Spree“
cards.body: Read the portrait as a magazine would print it. The five steps are the parts of a life story: Kindheit, Lehre, Wendepunkt, Neuanfang, heute. The past is told in the Präteritum, and today is in the Präsens. Find the five mixed verbs: dachte, brachte, kannte, nannten, wusste.
cards.lead: Now everything from the last three lessons comes together. Read the full portrait of Herr Ali and check each verb: regular, irregular, mixed, or present for today.
steps: Kindheit: Herr Ali wuchs in Zürich auf. Er lebte mit seiner Familie in der Nähe des Sees und kochte schon als Kind gern.
Lehre: Mit 16 machte er eine Lehre als Koch. Dann arbeitete er in einem Hotel in Basel. Er lernte viel, aber er dachte oft: Das ist nicht mein Leben.
Wendepunkt: Mit 25 verließ er die Schweiz. Er brachte nur eine Tasche und ein Rezept von seiner Großmutter mit. Er kannte in Berlin niemanden.
Neuanfang: Er fand ein kleines Zimmer und arbeitete in einer Küche. Die Kollegen nannten ihn bald „Chef“, denn er wusste immer, was die Gäste mochten.
Heute: Heute hat Herr Ali das Restaurant „Zum Löwen“. Er kocht noch jeden Tag, und viele Gäste kennen ihn.

examples.de: Die Kollegen nannten ihn bald „Chef“.
examples.en: His colleagues soon called him „Chef“.

examples.de: Heute hat Herr Ali das Restaurant „Zum Löwen“.
examples.en: Today Herr Ali runs the restaurant „Zum Löwen“.

deeper.text: Look at the small words schon and noch. Schon als Kind means already as a child, and noch jeden Tag means still every day. The portrait uses them to connect the past and the present: he cooked already as a child, and he still cooks today. These two words are a handy way to say that something started early or has not stopped.

example.de: Er kocht noch jeden Tag.
example.en: He still cooks every day.

cards.more: A portrait is like a bridge over a river. On the left bank stands the past, written in the Präteritum: wuchs, lebte, machte, kam. On the right bank stands today, written in the Präsens: hat, kocht. The word heute is the bridge, and you can see the tense change as soon as you cross it. Read the text twice. The first time, follow the story. The second time, underline all five mixed verbs with a coloured pen, and say each infinitive.

cards.title: Retelling and your own turn: telling a life story
cards.body: To retell a story, use the Präteritum for the story and the Präsens for today. Signal words guide the listener: damals, zunächst, dann, später, schließlich, heute. They take position 1, so the verb follows in position 2. Then change the nouns and tell your own turning point with the same frames.
cards.lead: You can read a life story, now you tell one. This card gives you the signal words that structure a story, and frames you can fill with your own life.

examples.de: Zunächst arbeitete er in einem Hotel.
examples.en: At first he worked in a hotel.

examples.de: Schließlich wurde das Restaurant bekannt.
examples.en: In the end the restaurant became well known.

examples.de: Mit 12 Jahren fing ich an, Gitarre zu spielen.
examples.en: At 12 I started to play the guitar.

examples.de: Damals dachte ich, dass Deutsch sehr schwer ist.
examples.en: At that time I thought that German was very hard.

deeper.text: Damals points to one moment in the past, früher to a time that was different from today, often with a habit: Früher kochte er nur für die Familie. Both words can start a sentence, and both need the verb in position 2. In a story you can use als to give a clear point in time: Als ich zwölf war, fing ich an, Bilder zu malen.

example.de: Als ich zwölf war, fing ich an, Bilder zu malen.
example.en: When I was twelve I started to paint pictures.

cards.more: Imagine a film trailer. A voice says: Damals … and you see grey pictures of the past. The voice continues with zunächst, dann, später, and each word is a new scene. Then the voice says: Heute … and the picture turns into colour. Your story works the same way. Avoid saying und over and over. Use the signposts instead. Take the frames Als Kind wohnte ich in … and Damals dachte ich, dass … and put your own life into them, or invent a life. The grammar is the same.

drills.prompt: Damals ___ Mira oft an Wien. (denken)
drills.hint: A mixed verb: new vowel and -te.
drills.explanation: Damals dachte Mira oft an Wien.

drills.prompt: Wir ___ nicht, dass er Koch war. (wissen)

lessons.title: Ich war, ich habe gemacht: Perfekt or Präteritum?
lessons.goal: Choose the past tense that fits the situation: Perfekt when you speak, Präteritum in writing, and always war, hatte and the modals.

grammar.point: Perfekt and Präteritum mean the same. In speaking, use the Perfekt (Ich habe gekocht). In stories, newspapers and reports, use the Präteritum (Leon kochte). The verbs sein, haben, werden, the modal verbs, wissen and es gibt stay in the Präteritum even when you speak: Ich war müde, Wir hatten Glück, Es gab Kuchen.
grammar.oneLine: Speaking: Perfekt. Writing: Präteritum. War, hatte, konnte: always.

mistake.wrong: Gestern habe ich keine Zeit gehabt, weil ich arbeiten gemusst habe.
mistake.right: Gestern hatte ich keine Zeit, weil ich arbeiten musste.
mistake.why: hatte and musste are always Präteritum, even in speech. The long Perfekt with gehabt and gemusst sounds odd.

terms.meaning: the past with haben or sein plus a participle at the end; the usual past in speaking
the one-word past (kochte, ging, war); the usual past in written stories and reports
colloquial language: how people really talk to each other

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich habe gekocht' to 'Leon kochte'
cards.body: You now own two ways to talk about the past: the Perfekt (habe gekocht) from A1 and the one-word Präteritum (kochte) from the last three lessons. Both say the same thing about time. Today you learn which one to pick, like choosing between a voice message and a newspaper.
steps: You already know: Ich habe gestern gekocht. Ich war müde. The Perfekt with a participle at the end, and war as one word.
New today: Leon kochte den ganzen Tag. The same past, but written. Today's question is not how, but when to use which.
By the end you can: pick the natural past for a chat, a story or a report, and say war, hatte and konnte even when you speak.

examples.de: Ich habe gestern gekocht.
examples.en: I cooked yesterday.
examples.why: You know this: Perfekt, the participle at the end.

examples.de: Ich war müde.
examples.en: I was tired.
examples.why: You know this too: one word for the past.

examples.de: Leon kochte den ganzen Tag.
examples.en: Leon cooked all day.
examples.why: New today: the one-word past, as you would read it in a text.

cards.more: Imagine two jackets in your wardrobe. One is a warm everyday jacket, the other is a smart coat for formal days. Both keep you warm, both are jackets. German has the same thing for the past. The Perfekt is the everyday jacket: you wear it when you talk. The Präteritum is the smart coat: you wear it in books, newspapers and reports. Today is the day you learn to look out of the window and choose the right one.

cards.title: Two pasts, one meaning: Perfekt and Präteritum
cards.body: Unlike English, German does not use its two pasts for different times. Ich habe gelebt and ich lebte both mean I lived. Perfekt: haben or sein plus a participle at the end. Präteritum: one word. The meaning stays the same, only the style changes: who tells the story, and where.
cards.lead: You know two ways to say the past. This card shows that they match one to one, so today's choice is about style and not about meaning.

examples.de: Mira hat in Wien gewohnt.
examples.en: Mira lived in Vienna.

examples.de: Mira wohnte in Wien.
examples.en: Mira lived in Vienna.

examples.de: Ben ist nach Berlin gezogen.
examples.en: Ben moved to Berlin.

examples.de: Ben zog nach Berlin.
examples.en: Ben moved to Berlin.

deeper.text: English splits the past: I have lived here for years is still true now, while I lived there is over. German does not. For something that is still true you use the Präsens with seit: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Berlin. For something that is over, Perfekt and Präteritum are equal in meaning. So you never ask which one is more past, only which one sounds right.

example.de: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Berlin.
example.en: I have been living in Berlin for two years.

cards.more: Picture a key that fits two doors. The door is the event: Herr Ali lived in Zürich. Behind door one the story sounds like talking, behind door two it sounds like reading. The key never changes the event, it only changes the mood of the room. Because of this, you do not have to think about time at all. Take any Perfekt sentence you know, say it as a Präteritum sentence, and the facts stay exactly the same. Only the sound changes.

cards.title: Speaking or writing? Your choice rule
cards.body: Ask two questions. Who is telling, and where? In a chat, on the phone or at the table you speak: use the Perfekt. In a novel, a fairy tale, a newspaper, a report or a biography you write: use the Präteritum. The story is the same, only the setting changes.
cards.lead: Now the rule you can use every day. Two quick questions tell you which past to choose, and every example shows one real situation.

examples.de: Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen.
examples.en: In a voice message: I went to the cinema yesterday.

examples.de: Es war einmal ein König.
examples.en: In a fairy tale: Once upon a time there was a king.

examples.de: Herr Ali wuchs in Zürich auf.
examples.en: In a biography: Herr Ali grew up in Zürich.

examples.de: Die Polizei fand das Fahrrad am Montag.
examples.en: In a newspaper: The police found the bike on Monday.

deeper.text: Written does not always mean Präteritum. A WhatsApp chat is written, but it sounds like speaking, so people use the Perfekt. The test is the voice, not the paper. The other way round, newsreaders on the radio speak in the Präteritum because they read a written text aloud. Ask yourself: does this sound like a person talking to a person, or like a text?

example.de: Der Bürgermeister eröffnete gestern die neue Brücke.
example.en: The mayor opened the new bridge yesterday.

cards.more: Think about clothes again, but now about places. At home you wear jeans. In the office you wear a suit. Nobody tells you the rule, you just look at where you are. The same works for the past. Look at where your sentence lives: on a phone screen, at a table, in a book, in a paper. Phone and table mean Perfekt. Book and paper mean Präteritum. If you stay unsure, the Perfekt is almost never wrong in a conversation.

rows: Herr Ali wuchs in Zürich auf.

steps: Question 1: Are you talking (voice message, phone, at the table)? Then choose the Perfekt.
Question 2: Is it a written text (Roman, Märchen, Zeitungsartikel, Bericht, Biografie)? Then choose the Präteritum.
Last check: is the verb war, hatte, wurde or a modal? Then read the next card.

cards.title: Always Präteritum: war, hatte, konnte and friends
cards.body: Some verbs stay in the Präteritum even when you speak: sein, haben, werden, the modal verbs, wissen and es gab. Their Perfekt is long and rare in speech. So you hear Ich war müde, Wir hatten Glück, Ich konnte nicht kommen and Es gab viele Leute all the time.
cards.lead: The choice rule has a famous exception. A handful of very short, very frequent verbs are always in the Präteritum, even in the middle of a spoken story.

examples.de: Wie war der Urlaub?
examples.en: How was the holiday?

examples.de: Toll! Wir hatten Glück mit dem Wetter und sind viel gewandert.
examples.en: Great! We were lucky with the weather and hiked a lot.

examples.de: Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen.
examples.en: I could not come yesterday.

examples.de: Es gab viele Leute, und ich wusste nicht, wo Mira war.
examples.en: There were many people, and I did not know where Mira was.

deeper.text: Some other short verbs are also very common in speech. You often hear dachte (Ich dachte, du kommst nicht), fand when it means think (Ich fand den Film gut) and ging in Es ging mir gut. These are not rules but habits. If you want a safe choice for any other verb in a chat, use the Perfekt and keep the six always-Präteritum verbs as they are.

example.de: Ich dachte, du kommst nicht.
example.en: I thought you were not coming.

cards.more: Here is a rule of thumb. The shorter and more frequent the verb, the more likely it stays in the Präteritum when you speak. War is one syllable, hatte is two, konnte is two. Compare Ich bin gewesen: that is so long and heavy that nobody chooses it. People are lazy when they talk, so they keep the short form. The long, rare verbs like wandern or kochen get the Perfekt, because their Präteritum sounds like a book.

cards.title: North, south, Austria, Switzerland: who says what
cards.body: Real German is not the same everywhere. In northern Germany you hear a little more Präteritum in speech. In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland people speak almost only in the Perfekt. Swiss German dialects have practically no Präteritum. In writing, everyone uses the Präteritum for stories.
cards.lead: A short culture card. It explains why Mira from Wien and Herr Ali from Zürich say so little in the Präteritum, even though they write it perfectly.

examples.de: Bei uns in Zürich sagt man: Ich bin gegangen.
examples.en: Herr Ali: Where I come from, in Zürich, we say: I went.

examples.de: Ich ging? Das sagt in Wien niemand.
examples.en: Mira: I went? Nobody says that in Vienna.

examples.de: Im Norden hört man gesprochenes Präteritum etwas öfter.
examples.en: In the north you hear spoken Präteritum a little more often.

deeper.text: The written language is the same in all of D-A-CH. A Swiss newspaper tells its stories in the Präteritum, and Swiss pupils learn to write it at school in Standard German. People simply switch when they switch from speaking to writing. Learners often notice the same switch in their own language, between how they talk to friends and how they write an essay.

example.de: Die Zeitung schrieb gestern über das Restaurant.
example.en: The newspaper wrote about the restaurant yesterday.

cards.more: Imagine Mira calls her mother in Wien. She says: Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen, und es war toll. Then she writes a story for her seminar: Sie ging ins Kino, und es war toll. Same person, same day, same film, two pasts. In the second text she sounds like a book, in the first one like a person. Nobody in Wien finds this strange. They switch without noticing, just like you switch between a text message and a letter.

rows: mostly Perfekt, a little more Präteritum

cards.title: One story, two versions: Leon's first day
cards.body: Here is one story in two settings. As a voice message to Mira, Leon uses the Perfekt. As a short report in a newsletter, the same sentences use the Präteritum. Only the verbs change: helper plus participle becomes one single word. War stays war.
cards.lead: Now you do it yourself. Leon's first day in Herr Ali's kitchen appears twice, once spoken and once written, so you can see exactly how each sentence changes.

examples.de: Ich bin um sieben ins Restaurant gekommen.
examples.en: Spoken: I came to the restaurant at seven.

examples.de: Leon kam um sieben ins Restaurant.
examples.en: Written: Leon came to the restaurant at seven.

examples.de: Herr Ali hat mir eine Schürze gegeben.
examples.en: Spoken: Herr Ali gave me an apron.

examples.de: Herr Ali gab ihm eine Schürze.
examples.en: Written: Herr Ali gave them an apron.

deeper.text: Separable verbs show the change most clearly. In the Perfekt the participle stays in one piece at the end: Ich bin um sieben angekommen. In the Präteritum the verb splits, and the small part goes to the end: Leon kam um sieben an. So the frame for ankommen is bin ... angekommen in speech, but kam ... an in a text.

example.de: Leon kam um sieben an.
example.en: Leon arrived at seven.

cards.more: Think of building blocks. In the Perfekt you use two blocks: a helper (hat, ist) and a participle (gegeben, gekommen). In the Präteritum you use only one block: gab, kam. So changing a Perfekt sentence to the Präteritum is a swap of two blocks for one, and the little word order stays the same: the verb is in position 2. Try it with every sentence and you will soon do it without thinking.

rows: Ich bin um sieben ins Restaurant gekommen.
Leon kam um sieben ins Restaurant.
Herr Ali hat mir eine Schürze gegeben.
Herr Ali gab ihm eine Schürze.
Am Abend war ich sehr müde.
Am Abend war Leon sehr müde.

steps: Find the helper and the participle: hat gegeben.
Replace both by one Präteritum word: gab.
Put it in position 2. Nothing stays at the end, except a small part of a separable verb.

cards.title: One verb, one tense: the two traps
cards.body: Two traps. First: do not build a long Perfekt for the always-Präteritum verbs: Ich habe nicht gekonnt sounds odd, say Ich konnte nicht. Second: in a text, do not jump between tenses for no reason. Choose the Präteritum for a written story, or the Perfekt for a spoken one, and stay with it.
cards.lead: A last card about mistakes. Both traps are easy to avoid once you know them, and the first one is the mistake you will hear most from learners.

examples.de: Gestern hatte ich keine Zeit, weil ich arbeiten musste.
examples.en: Yesterday I had no time because I had to work.

examples.de: Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen.
examples.en: I could not come yesterday.

examples.de: Wir sind nach Hause gegangen, und es war schon spät.
examples.en: We walked home and it was already late.

deeper.text: A spoken story mixes both tenses and that is normal. Ich war gestern in der Stadt und habe Anna getroffen: war is the always-Präteritum verb, habe getroffen is the Perfekt for everything else. In a written text you use the Präteritum for all of it: Ich war gestern in der Stadt und traf Anna. So the mix in speech is not a mistake, it is the rule.

example.de: Ich war gestern in der Stadt und habe Anna getroffen.
example.en: I was in town yesterday and met Anna.

cards.more: Think of cooking with two pans. A pan for speaking (Perfekt) and a pan for writing (Präteritum). The always-Präteritum verbs are a small spoon that goes into both pans: war, hatte, konnte. The mistake is to cook the spoon in the Perfekt pan, as in gekonnt. Another mistake is to cook half the soup in one pan and half in the other for no reason. Choose a pan, cook the whole soup in it, and keep the spoon the same.

lessons.title: Was macht dich glücklich?: talking about happiness
lessons.goal: Say what makes you happy with three sentence frames, tell the difference between Glück haben and glücklich sein, and tell a lucky moment in the right past.

grammar.topic: Talking about happiness: Glück haben or glücklich sein
grammar.point: Glück haben means to be lucky, glücklich sein means to be happy. Three frames say what makes you happy: Mich macht … glücklich. Ich bin glücklich, wenn … Es macht mich glücklich, … zu …. A lucky moment is told with hatte or war and the Perfekt.
grammar.oneLine: Ich hatte Glück. Ich bin glücklich, wenn die Sonne scheint.

mistake.wrong: Ich bin Glück in der Prüfung.
mistake.right: Ich hatte Glück in der Prüfung.
mistake.why: To be lucky is Glück haben (a noun). To be happy is glücklich sein (an adjective).

terms.meaning: a short, strong feeling of happiness
contentment: a long, quiet feeling that your life is good
a verb used as a noun: das Malen, das Kochen (neuter, capital letter)

cards.title: Before we start: one word, two meanings: Glück
cards.body: Mira and Leon are making a radio show called „Wendepunkte“ about changes in life and about happiness. For the show Mira wants to ask people: What makes you happy? In German the word Glück means both happiness and luck, so today you learn to tell the two apart and to answer the question in full sentences.
steps: You already know: glücklich, zufrieden and sich freuen from A2, and Pech haben for bad luck.
New today: Glück haben (to be lucky) is not the same as glücklich sein (to be happy), plus three sentence frames to say what makes you happy.
By the end you can: answer the question Was macht dich glücklich? and tell a short lucky moment from your week.

examples.de: Ich bin heute glücklich.
examples.en: I am happy today.
examples.why: You know this: glücklich with sein.

examples.de: Ich habe mich auf das Wochenende gefreut.
examples.en: I was happy about the weekend.
examples.why: You know this too: sich freuen.

examples.de: Ich hatte Glück mit dem Wetter.
examples.en: I was lucky with the weather.
examples.why: New today: Glück haben means to be lucky, not to be happy.

cards.more: Imagine two small boxes. In box one lives a feeling: you are glücklich, warm inside, maybe you smile. In box two lives a lucky chance: the bus waited for you, you found your phone, you had Glück. English uses two words, happy and lucky. German uses one family of words for both. Do not worry: the verb tells you which box you are in. Sein plus glücklich is the feeling box. Haben plus Glück is the chance box.

cards.title: Glück: happiness and luck
cards.body: Glück is one noun with two meanings. As a feeling it is happiness: Ich bin glücklich. As a chance it is luck: Ich habe Glück. Notice the verbs: sein with the adjective glücklich, haben with the noun Glück. Zum Glück and glücklicherweise both mean luckily.
cards.lead: The first box is Glück itself. These examples keep the two meanings next to each other so you can hear the difference between feeling and chance.

examples.de: Mira ist heute glücklich.
examples.en: Mira is happy today.

examples.de: Leon hatte Glück in der Prüfung.
examples.en: Leon was lucky in the exam.

examples.de: Zum Glück war das Wetter schön.
examples.en: Luckily the weather was nice.

examples.de: Ben ist ein Glückspilz.
examples.en: Ben is a lucky person.

deeper.text: Glück is almost always singular, and Glück haben has no article. Do not mix it up with Glückwunsch, which means congratulations: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag! You wish someone Viel Glück when something important begins, for example an exam, and Glückwunsch when something good has happened. So Viel Glück! is before, Glückwunsch is after.

example.de: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!
example.en: Congratulations on your birthday!

cards.more: Picture a lottery ticket and a sunny day. The ticket in your hand is chance: you have it or you do not, like Glück haben and Pech haben. The sunny feeling in your chest is mood: you are it, like glücklich sein. German uses the same stem because in old German the two ideas were one. You do not need history for this. Just remember: haben goes with the ticket, sein goes with the sun. And a Glückspilz is somebody who always wins the ticket.

rows: Ich hatte Glück mit dem Wetter.
Zum Glück war das Wetter schön.

cards.title: What makes you happy? Three sentence frames
cards.body: Mira asks people on the campus: Was macht dich glücklich? There are three easy frames. Mich macht … glücklich. Ich bin glücklich, wenn … (verb at the end). Es macht mich glücklich, … zu … (the infinitive with zu at the end). Pick one and fill the gap with your own answer.
cards.lead: Now the question of the radio show. Six people on the campus gave six different answers, and each answer uses one of the three frames, so you can copy them.

examples.de: Mich macht Zeit mit Freunden glücklich.
examples.en: Time with friends makes me happy.

examples.de: Ich bin glücklich, wenn die Sonne scheint.
examples.en: I am happy when the sun shines.

examples.de: Es macht mich glücklich, morgens einen Kaffee in der Sonne zu trinken.
examples.en: It makes me happy to drink a coffee in the sun in the morning.

examples.de: Ich bin dankbar für meine Gesundheit.
examples.en: I am grateful for my health.

deeper.text: The zu-part can also stand at the beginning, and then it replaces es. Instead of Es macht mich glücklich, für andere zu kochen you can say Für andere zu kochen macht mich glücklich. The whole zu-part counts as position 1, so macht follows right after it. Both versions are common. The version with es is a bit easier to say, because you know early what the sentence is about.

example.de: Für andere zu kochen macht mich glücklich.
example.en: Cooking for others makes me happy.

cards.more: Think of three keys on a key ring. The first key opens a small door: Mich macht Familie glücklich, short and direct. The second key opens a door with a condition: Ich bin glücklich, wenn … and the verb waits at the end. The third key opens a door with an action: Es macht mich glücklich, … zu …. A good radio answer uses one key, adds a reason and stops. You do not need all three keys for every answer.

rows: Mich macht Zeit mit Freunden glücklich.
Ich bin glücklich, wenn ich gesund bin.
Es macht mich glücklich, für andere zu kochen.
Ich bin glücklich, wenn ich in der Sonne einen Kaffee trinke.

steps: Choose your answer: Familie, Gesundheit, Freunde, Arbeit, a small thing.
Choose a frame: Mich macht … / Ich bin glücklich, wenn … / Es macht mich glücklich, … zu …
Add one reason with weil or denn.

cards.title: Glücksgefühl or Zufriedenheit?
cards.body: A Glücksgefühl is a short, strong feeling: good news, a great note, a surprise. Zufriedenheit is a long, quiet feeling: your life is good as it is. Two helpers belong here. Dankbar sein für means to be thankful for, and genießen means to enjoy. Both are verbs of a calm mind.
cards.lead: Not all happiness is the same. This card separates the short flash from the long glow, and gives you words for the quiet kind.

examples.de: Ein Glücksgefühl dauert oft nur kurz.
examples.en: A feeling of happiness often lasts only a short time.

examples.de: Zufriedenheit bleibt länger.
examples.en: Contentment stays longer.

examples.de: Ich bin dankbar für meine Freunde.
examples.en: I am grateful for my friends.

examples.de: Mira genießt den Abend.
examples.en: Mira enjoys the evening.

deeper.text: German has two nice sayings here. Glück im Unglück means a blessing in disguise: something bad happens, but it could have been worse. And Scherben bringen Glück: at a Polterabend, the party on the evening before a wedding, guests break old porcelain, and the shards are supposed to bring luck. Never break the plates of a restaurant, though.

example.de: Scherben bringen Glück.
example.en: Shards bring luck.

cards.more: Fireworks and candles are a good picture. A firework is bright, loud and over in seconds: that is a Glücksgefühl. A candle is small, but it burns all evening: that is Zufriedenheit. Both are nice. Many people say a good life needs a lot of candles and a few fireworks. And dankbar sein is the match that lights the candle: when you notice what you already have, the calm feeling starts.

rows: a good life, a good year

cards.title: A lucky moment, told in the Perfekt
cards.body: You tell a lucky moment the way you speak. The frame uses war or hatte, the events use the Perfekt, and the feeling uses war again. This is the rule from today's first lesson in use: Ich hatte Glück: Ich habe mein Handy verloren, und ein Mann hat es gefunden.
cards.lead: Time to use the Perfekt rule. This card tells one small lucky moment as a voice message, so you can hear how war, hatte and the Perfekt work together.

examples.de: Ich hatte letzte Woche Glück: Ich habe mein Handy verloren, und ein Mann hat es gefunden.
examples.en: Last week I was lucky: I lost my phone, and a man found it.

examples.de: Zum Glück war der Mann sehr nett.
examples.en: Luckily the man was very nice.

examples.de: Ich war so glücklich, und wir haben zusammen einen Kaffee getrunken.
examples.en: I was so happy, and we drank a coffee together.

deeper.text: After a lucky moment people often say Glück gehabt! or Da habe ich aber Glück gehabt! This is the Perfekt of haben, and it is a fixed phrase, so it does not break the rule from before. You can also use a short exclamation without any verb: So ein Glück! Such short phrases are very typical for spoken German.

example.de: Da habe ich aber Glück gehabt!
example.en: I was really lucky there!

cards.more: Think of a sandwich. The top slice is the frame: Ich hatte Glück, war and hatte, because they stay in the Präteritum. The filling is the story: what happened, in the Perfekt, with habe verloren and hat gefunden. The bottom slice is the feeling at the end: Ich war so glücklich. If you build all your lucky stories like this sandwich, you will always have the right tense, and the listener always knows where the story starts and ends.

cards.title: In the WG kitchen: a dialogue
cards.body: Mira collects answers for „Wendepunkte“ in the kitchen of the WG. Each friend uses another frame. Read the dialogue aloud and look at the colours. Which frame does each person use? And where is the verb in each sentence?
cards.lead: Here you hear the frames in a real conversation. Eight short lines from the WG kitchen show how natural they sound when friends talk.

examples.de: Mira: Ich schreibe Fragen für unsere Sendung „Wendepunkte“. Was macht euch glücklich?
examples.en: Mira: I am writing questions for our show „Wendepunkte“. What makes you happy?

examples.de: Anna: Malen macht mich glücklich. Wenn ich male, bin ich ganz ruhig.
examples.en: Anna: Painting makes me happy. When I paint, I am completely calm.

examples.de: Ben: Ich bin ein Glückspilz: Ich habe Anna, und ich habe gute Freunde.
examples.en: Ben: I am a lucky person: I have Anna, and I have good friends.

examples.de: Leon: Mich macht Kochen für andere glücklich.
examples.en: Leon: Cooking for others makes me happy.

examples.de: Mira: Und was macht dich zufrieden, Leon? Ist das etwas anderes?
examples.en: Mira: And what makes you content, Leon? Is that something different?

examples.de: Leon: Ja! Glück ist ein Moment. Zufriedenheit bleibt länger, zum Beispiel nach einem guten Tag.
examples.en: Leon: Yes! Happiness is a moment. Contentment stays longer, for example after a good day.

examples.de: Anna: Mira, schreib auch: Es macht mich glücklich, morgens in Ruhe Kaffee zu trinken.
examples.en: Anna: Mira, write this too: It makes me happy to drink coffee in peace in the morning.

examples.de: Mira: Super, das ist meine erste Antwort für die Umfrage!
examples.en: Mira: Great, that is my first answer for the survey!

deeper.text: Malen and Kochen are verbs used as nouns. Any infinitive can become a noun: das Malen, das Kochen, das Laufen. It is always neuter, it has a capital letter and no plural. That is why Anna can start with Malen macht mich glücklich. With an article it sounds a little more careful: Das Laufen am Morgen macht mich glücklich.

example.de: Das Laufen am Morgen macht mich glücklich.
example.en: Running in the morning makes me happy.

cards.more: Try the dialogue like an actor. First read only Mira's lines, so you hear the questions. Then read only the answers and underline the verb in each one. You will see it always comes right after the first element, or at the very end after wenn. The third step is the best: change one detail, for example Leon's cooking into your own hobby, and read the line again. That is how you turn a dialogue into your own sentences.

cards.title: Reading: Kleine Dinge, großes Glück
cards.body: Lena sends a message to the campus radio. Read it sentence by sentence. Strategy: find the reason words. Weil sends the verb to the end, denn does not change the word order, and deshalb is followed by the verb. These small words tell you why somebody is happy.
cards.lead: The last card is a short listener message. It is real, simple German with all the reason words from this chapter, and you can read it in one minute.

examples.de: Hallo Campusradio, ich bin Lena und studiere Medizin.
examples.en: Hello campus radio, I am Lena and I study medicine.

examples.de: Mein Alltag ist stressig, deshalb freue ich mich über kleine Dinge.
examples.en: My everyday life is stressful, so I enjoy small things.

examples.de: Morgens trinke ich einen Kaffee auf dem Balkon, denn dann ist es ruhig.
examples.en: In the morning I drink a coffee on the balcony, because then it is quiet.

examples.de: Ich bin glücklich, wenn die Sonne scheint.
examples.en: I am happy when the sun shines.

examples.de: Gestern hatte ich Glück: Der Bus war noch da, weil der Fahrer auf mich gewartet hat.
examples.en: Yesterday I was lucky: the bus was still there, because the driver waited for me.

examples.de: Das war nur ein kleiner Moment, aber ich war den ganzen Tag froh.
examples.en: That was only a small moment, but I was happy all day.

examples.de: Für mich ist das Zufriedenheit: Man braucht nicht viel.
examples.en: For me that is contentment: you do not need much.

examples.de: Viele Grüße Lena
examples.en: Best wishes, Lena

deeper.text: Denn and weil both mean because, but they behave differently. Denn does not change the word order: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin müde. Weil sends the verb to the end: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin. In speech many people use weil with the verb in position 2: Weil ich bin müde. You will hear this a lot, but in writing and in exams use the verb at the end.

example.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin müde.
example.en: I stay at home, because I am tired.

cards.more: Be a detective and look for the reason words. Take a pencil and circle every weil, denn and deshalb in Lena's message. Each circle is a clue that answers Warum? Why is she happy? Why was the day good? When you have circled all of them, close the text and tell the story in three sentences with your own words. You will notice that you understand much more than you thought, because the little words carry the logic of the text.
